lessons.title: Place Value: Tens and Ones
lessons.subject: Math
lessons.reading_material: Numbers bigger than 10 have two parts: TENS and ONES. In the number 35, the 3 is in the tens place (meaning 3 groups of ten = 30) and the 5 is in the ones place (meaning 5 ones). So 35 = 30 + 5. We use a place value chart to organise digits.
practical_activities: Build 2-digit numbers with base-ten blocks
Play 'make the number' with digit cards
Order numbers on a number line to 100

exercises.q: Write 5 tens and 3 ones as a number.

homework.task: Write the tens and ones in: 28, 45, 63, 71, 90

revision.notes: Place value: Tens position × 10 + Ones position. 47 = 4×10 + 7 = 47.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

questions.q: What is the value of 6 in 67?

lessons.title: Addition to 100
lessons.subject: Math
learning_objectives: Add 2-digit numbers with and without regrouping
lessons.reading_material: Now we add bigger numbers! 34 + 25: add ones first (4+5=9), then tens (3+2=5), so 34+25=59. Sometimes we need to 'regroup' or 'carry': 37+45, ones: 7+5=12 (write 2, carry 1 ten), tens: 3+4+1=8, answer: 82. Always check by starting from the beginning!
practical_activities: Add with base-ten blocks showing regrouping
Mental maths: add tens first strategy
Estimation: round to nearest ten then add

revision.notes: Column addition: ones first, then tens. Regroup when ones sum ≥ 10.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Subtraction to 100
lessons.subject: Math
learning_objectives: Subtract 2-digit numbers with and without borrowing
lessons.reading_material: Subtraction with big numbers uses 'borrowing'. 73 − 47: ones: 3−7 not possible, borrow a ten from 7 (now 6 tens and 13 ones): 13−7=6 ones, 6−4=2 tens. Answer: 26. Always check: 26+47=73 ✓
practical_activities: Subtract with base-ten blocks
Number line subtraction jumps
Solve real-life shopping subtraction problems

revision.notes: Subtraction with borrowing: if ones too small, borrow 1 ten → 10 ones. Check with addition.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Introduction to Multiplication
lessons.subject: Math
lessons.reading_material: Multiplication is a quick way to add the same number many times. Instead of 3+3+3+3, we write 4×3=12. The '×' means 'groups of'. 4×3 means 4 groups of 3. Let's learn the 2 times table: 1×2=2, 2×2=4, 3×2=6... and the 5 times table: 1×5=5, 2×5=10, 3×5=15...
practical_activities: Array activities (rows and columns)
Skip counting for multiplication
Times tables chant for 2s and 5s

homework.task: Write all the 2× and 5× facts. Practice until you know them.

revision.notes: Multiplication: repeated addition. 3×4 = 3+3+3+3 = 12. Array shows rows and columns.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Fractions: Halves and Quarters
lessons.subject: Math
learning_objectives: Identify halves and quarters of shapes
lessons.reading_material: A fraction is part of a whole. When we cut a pizza into 2 equal pieces, each piece is ONE HALF (1/2). When we cut into 4 equal pieces, each piece is ONE QUARTER (1/4). The bottom number (denominator) shows how many equal parts total. The top number (numerator) shows how many parts we have.
practical_activities: Fold paper into halves and quarters
Share food equally into fractions
Shade fraction diagrams

exercises.q: What fraction is shaded if 1 of 4 equal parts is coloured?

homework.task: Fold 2 sheets of paper: one in half, one in quarters. Colour fractions.

revision.notes: Half (1/2) = 1 of 2 equal parts. Quarter (1/4) = 1 of 4 equal parts. Halves > quarters.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Money
lessons.subject: Math
lessons.reading_material: Money is used to buy and sell things. We use coins and notes. A 1p coin is worth 1 penny. A 5p coin is worth 5 pennies. A 10p coin is worth 10p. A 50p coin is worth 50p. A £1 coin is worth 100p. When you buy something, change = amount paid − price.
practical_activities: Sort and count coin collections
Shop roleplay with class store
Calculate change for simple purchases

exercises.q: If something costs 30p and you pay 50p, what change do you get?

homework.task: Create a mini price list for 5 toys. Calculate how much 2 items cost together.

revision.notes: Add coin values to find total. Change = payment − cost. Always check: cost + change = payment.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Reading: Fiction and Non-Fiction
lessons.subject: English
learning_objectives: Use a contents page and index
lessons.reading_material: Books can be FICTION (made-up stories) or NON-FICTION (true information). Fiction has characters, settings, plots, and is imagined. Non-fiction books have: CONTENTS PAGE (shows what's in the book and page numbers), INDEX (alphabetical list at the back), HEADINGS, PHOTOGRAPHS/diagrams. A dictionary, encyclopaedia, and science book are non-fiction.
practical_activities: Sort books into fiction and non-fiction
Use contents page to find information
Write a non-fiction fact file

exercises.q: What does an index help you find?
exercises.answer: Specific topics or words and their page numbers

homework.task: Choose a non-fiction book. Write 5 facts you learned. Note which page each came from.

revision.notes: Fiction=imagined. Non-fiction=true information. Contents=front. Index=back. Headings organise information.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Grammar: Adjectives and Adverbs
lessons.subject: English
learning_objectives: Use adjectives to expand noun phrases
lessons.reading_material: We learned adjectives describe nouns. Now meet ADVERBS! Adverbs describe VERBS — they tell us HOW, WHEN, or WHERE. Many adverbs end in '-ly': quickly, quietly, suddenly, carefully. 'She ran quickly' — quickly tells us HOW she ran. Adjectives: big, red, happy, cold. Adverbs: quickly, loudly, here, yesterday. Together they make writing much richer!
practical_activities: Add adjectives and adverbs to boring sentences
Adverb mime game
Descriptive writing competition

homework.task: Take 5 boring sentences and improve them by adding at least one adjective and one adverb each.

revision.notes: Adjective: describes noun. Adverb: describes verb (often -ly). They expand and improve our writing.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

questions.q: 'The cat walked slowly' — what is the adverb?

lessons.title: States of Matter
lessons.subject: Science
lessons.reading_material: Matter is everything around us. Matter can be solid (fixed shape), liquid (takes shape of container), or gas (fills all available space). Ice is solid, water is liquid, steam is gas.
practical_activities: Feel solid objects
Pour water into different containers
Blow up a balloon

homework.task: List 3 solids, 3 liquids, 3 gases at home

revision.notes: Solid=fixed shape; Liquid=no fixed shape; Gas=no fixed shape or volume.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: The Water Cycle
lessons.subject: Science
lessons.reading_material: Water moves in a cycle. The sun heats water → evaporation (water becomes vapor). Vapor rises, cools → condensation (forms clouds). Clouds get heavy → precipitation (rain/snow). Water flows back to rivers and oceans.
practical_activities: Demonstrate evaporation with a wet cloth in sunlight
Draw the water cycle

homework.task: Observe a puddle at school for one week — does it get smaller?

revision.notes: Sun → Evaporation → Condensation → Precipitation → back to start.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Continents and Oceans
lessons.subject: Geography
lessons.reading_material: Earth has 7 continents: Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, South America, Australia/Oceania, Antarctica. The 5 oceans are Pacific (largest), Atlantic, Indian, Southern, Arctic. Continents are large landmasses; oceans are huge bodies of salt water.
practical_activities: Label a world map with continents and oceans
Sort country cards to their continents

homework.task: Colour and label a world map with continents

revision.notes: 7 continents, 5 oceans. Pacific = largest. Antarctica = southernmost.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Weather and Climate
lessons.subject: Geography
lessons.reading_material: Weather is the day-to-day condition of the atmosphere (sunny, rainy, windy). Climate is the average weather over many years for a region. Tropical climates near the equator are hot and wet. Polar climates near the poles are cold. Temperate climates have four seasons.
practical_activities: Keep a weather diary for one week
Match climate zones to regions on a world map

homework.task: Research what type of climate your country has

revision.notes: Weather = now; Climate = long-term average.

lessons.title: Myths and Legends
lessons.subject: World Literature
learning_objectives: Retell a Greek or Norse myth
lessons.reading_material: Myths are ancient stories used to explain the world — why the sun rises, how fire was created, where the seasons come from. Greek myths: Prometheus stole fire for humans. Persephone explains why we have winter. Norse myths: Odin, Thor, and Loki are gods in Viking stories. Legends are stories about real (or partly real) heroes that have grown over time: King Arthur in Britain, Robin Hood, Sundiata Keita of Mali. Both myths and legends reveal what a culture values.
practical_activities: Act out the myth of Prometheus — one student is Prometheus, others are Zeus's guards
exercises: What is the difference between a myth and a legend?
Explain what the myth of Persephone tells us about seasons

learning_objectives: Mix colours to make new colours

lessons.title: Rhythm and Beat
lessons.subject: Music
lessons.reading_material: The BEAT is the steady pulse in music (like a heartbeat). RHYTHM is the pattern of long and short sounds. TEMPO is the speed — fast music is allegro, slow music is adagio.

lessons.homework: Listen to two contrasting songs — one fast, one slow. Describe how tempo changes the feel.

revision.notes: The BEAT is like a clock — it never changes. The RHYTHM dances on top of the beat.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

info_cards.title: Famous Person: Leonardo da Vinci
info_cards.fact: Leonardo da Vinci was an Italian artist and inventor who painted the Mona Lisa and filled notebooks with designs for flying machines centuries before airplanes existed.

info_cards.title: Book Summary: A Brief History of Time
info_cards.fact: "A Brief History of Time" by physicist Stephen Hawking (1988) explains big ideas about the universe — like black holes and the Big Bang — in everyday language.

info_cards.fact: "The Story of My Life" by Helen Keller is the memoir of how Helen Keller, who was deaf and blind from infancy, learned to read, write, and communicate.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Marie Curie
info_cards.fact: "Nothing in life is to be feared, it is only to be understood." — Polish-French physicist and chemist who discovered the elements polonium and radium and won two Nobel Prizes.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Albert Einstein
info_cards.fact: "Imagination is more important than knowledge." — German-born physicist who developed the theory of relativity and won the Nobel Prize in Physics.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Leonardo da Vinci
info_cards.fact: "Simplicity is the ultimate sophistication." — Italian Renaissance painter, engineer, and scientist who painted the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
info_cards.fact: "Neither a lofty degree of intelligence nor imagination... is essential to genius. Love, love, love, that is the soul of genius." — Austrian composer who wrote over 600 works and is considered one of the greatest composers in Western music history.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Ludwig van Beethoven
info_cards.fact: "Music can change the world." — German composer who continued composing symphonies even after losing his hearing.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Galileo Galilei
info_cards.fact: "I have never met a man so ignorant that I couldn't learn something from him." — Italian astronomer and physicist who improved the telescope and supported the idea that Earth orbits the Sun.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Isaac Newton
info_cards.fact: "If I have seen further it is by standing on the shoulders of giants." — English physicist and mathematician who described the laws of motion and universal gravitation.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Charles Darwin
info_cards.fact: "It is not the strongest of the species that survives, but the most adaptable." — English naturalist whose theory of evolution by natural selection was published in On the Origin of Species.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Alexander Graham Bell
info_cards.fact: "Before anything else, preparation is the key to success." — Scottish-born inventor credited with patenting the first practical telephone.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Thomas Edison
info_cards.fact: "I have not failed. I've just found 10,000 ways that won't work." — American inventor credited with developing the practical electric light bulb and the phonograph.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Nikola Tesla
info_cards.fact: "The present is theirs; the future, for which I really worked, is mine." — Serbian-American inventor and engineer who pioneered alternating-current (AC) electrical systems.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Rosalind Franklin
info_cards.fact: "Science and everyday life cannot and should not be separated." — British chemist whose X-ray images were crucial to discovering the structure of DNA.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Katherine Johnson
info_cards.fact: "Like any survivor, I'm grateful to have been knocked down... It only made me work harder." — American mathematician whose calculations were vital to NASA's early human spaceflight missions.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: George Washington Carver
info_cards.fact: "Education is the key to unlock the golden door of freedom." — American agricultural scientist who developed hundreds of new uses for the peanut and other crops.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Frederick Douglass
info_cards.fact: "Once you learn to read, you will be forever free." — American social reformer who escaped slavery and became a leading abolitionist writer and speaker.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Harriet Tubman
info_cards.fact: "Every great dream begins with a dreamer." — American abolitionist who escaped slavery and led dozens of others to freedom via the Underground Railroad.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Sojourner Truth
info_cards.fact: "Truth is powerful and it prevails." — American abolitionist and women's rights activist born into slavery, known for her speech 'Ain't I a Woman?'

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Booker T. Washington
info_cards.fact: "Success is to be measured not so much by the position one has reached in life as by the obstacles overcome." — American educator who founded the Tuskegee Institute to provide education for African Americans.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Susan B. Anthony
info_cards.fact: "Failure is impossible." — American activist who fought for women's right to vote and helped found the National Woman Suffrage Association.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Elizabeth Cady Stanton
info_cards.fact: "The moment we begin to fear the opinions of others... we have begun to die." — American women's rights leader who co-organized the 1848 Seneca Falls Convention.

lessons.title: Hello in Arabic!
lessons.subject: Foreign Languages
learning_objectives: Say hello and goodbye in Arabic
lessons.reading_material: Arabic is spoken by over 300 million people and is one of the official languages of the United Nations. In Arabic, we say 'مرحبا' (Marhaba) for hello and 'مع السلامة' (Ma'a as-salama) for goodbye. Numbers: واحد، اثنان، ثلاثة، أربعة، خمسة، ستة، سبعة، ثمانية، تسعة، عشرة (1–10). Arabic is written right to left.
practical_activities: Greet a partner in Arabic three times using different times of day (morning/afternoon/evening)
exercises: Write the Arabic numbers 1–10
How do you say 'My name is…' in Arabic (اسمي…)?
Write the Arabic greeting for 'Good morning' (صباح الخير)
lessons.homework: Practise writing your name in Arabic transliteration.

revision.notes: Marhaba=hello, Ma'a as-salama=goodbye, Ismī=my name is. Numbers 1-10 in Arabic.
revision.tip: Repeat greetings aloud — pronunciation improves with practice.

quiz.question: How do you say 'Hello' in Arabic?

lessons.assessment: Introduce yourself in Arabic (name, age, school) — 3 sentences minimum.

lessons.title: Needs and Wants
lessons.subject: Social Studies
learning_objectives: Give examples of needs and wants
lessons.reading_material: Needs are things we must have to survive: food, water, shelter, clothing, and healthcare. Wants are things we would like to have but can live without: toys, sweets, video games. Because resources are limited, we must make choices about what to spend money and time on. This is called scarcity — we cannot have everything we want, so we prioritise.
practical_activities: Sorting activity: sort 20 picture cards into 'needs' and 'wants' columns — discuss edge cases
exercises: List 3 needs and 3 wants
Why can't we always have everything we want?
What is scarcity?
lessons.homework: Make a 'needs vs wants' journal — for one week, note which things you buy are needs and which are wants.

revision.notes: Needs = survival essentials. Wants = desired extras. Scarcity means we must choose.
revision.tip: Ask: 'Would I survive without this?' — if yes, it's a want.

quiz.question: Scarcity means
options: Having to make choices because resources are limited
quiz.correct: Having to make choices because resources are limited

lessons.assessment: Give 3 examples of needs and 3 of wants from your own life.

lessons.title: Body Awareness and Movement
lessons.subject: Physical Education & Self-Defense
learning_objectives: Name major muscle groups and body parts
lessons.reading_material: Our bodies are amazing — they can run, jump, balance, and throw. Exercise keeps our heart, muscles, and bones strong. Learning how our body moves is the first step to being physically active for life.
practical_activities: Body part warm-up: touch and name each body part
Obstacle course using different locomotor skills
exercises: Name 3 muscles you feel when running
Explain why exercise is good for your heart
lessons.homework: Try 3 different types of exercise and describe which muscles each one uses.

revision.notes: Your heart is a muscle — exercise makes it stronger so it pumps blood more efficiently.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.assessment: Perform and describe 4 different locomotor movements.

info_cards.title: Local government
info_cards.fact: Towns and cities have leaders called mayors. They help make rules for the community.

info_cards.title: Voting
info_cards.fact: Grown-ups vote to choose their leaders. Everyone gets one vote.

lessons.title: My Community
lessons.subject: Civics
learning_objectives: Describe how people work together in a community
lessons.reading_material: A community is a group of people living and working together. Community helpers: doctors, teachers, police, firefighters, shopkeepers. Each person plays a role. When we cooperate and help each other, the community is strong.
practical_activities: Interview a community helper (virtual or in person)
Map your community's key places and services

homework.task: Write a thank-you card to a community helper

revision.notes: Community = people working together. Helpers provide services. Cooperation makes it strong.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

info_cards.title: Food groups
info_cards.fact: A balanced diet includes fruits, vegetables, grains, proteins, and dairy.

info_cards.title: Water
info_cards.fact: Drink 6-8 glasses of water a day. Our bodies are about 60% water.

quiz_bank.question: Which food group includes apples and oranges?

lessons.title: Healthy Habits
lessons.subject: Health Education
lessons.reading_material: Healthy habits keep our bodies and minds well. Key habits: washing hands, eating vegetables and fruit, drinking water, getting enough sleep (9-11 hours for children), and being active every day.
practical_activities: Create a healthy day schedule
Discuss why eating breakfast matters
exercises: List 5 healthy habits
Explain what happens when we don't get enough sleep
lessons.homework: Plan a full day of healthy choices from waking up to bedtime.

revision.notes: Sleep is not wasted time — your brain consolidates learning and your body repairs itself while you sleep.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

info_cards.title: Software
info_cards.body: Software is the set of instructions that tells a computer what to do. Games, apps, and word processors are all software.

info_cards.title: Hardware
info_cards.body: Hardware is the physical parts of a computer you can touch, like the keyboard, screen, and mouse.

info_cards.title: Internet Safety
info_cards.body: Never share your name, address, or phone number with strangers online. Always ask a trusted adult before visiting a new website.

quiz_bank.q: What is the physical part of a computer called?

lessons.title: Introduction to the Internet
lessons.subject: ICT & Computer Science
lessons.reading_material: The internet is a huge network connecting computers worldwide. A browser (Chrome, Firefox) lets you visit websites. A URL is the website address. Online safety: never share personal information, always ask an adult before downloading.
practical_activities: Practise typing a URL into a browser
Identify safe vs unsafe online behaviour scenarios

homework.task: Ask a parent to help you visit an educational website and name what you learned

revision.notes: Internet = global network. Browser = tool to access websites. Safety = no personal info online.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class
